title: Thackeray Cousins Unite, Announce Joint March in Mumbai on July 26 Over NEET Crisis
excerpt: Uddhav and Raj Thackeray set aside political differences to back students protesting NEET paper leaks and police crackdowns, with a march planned from Shivaji Park to Siddhivinayak temple.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Uddhav and Raj Thackeray will march in Mumbai on July 26 to support NEET protestors.
  • The march will start at Shivaji Park and end at Siddhivinayak temple, without political flags.
  • Mumbai police imposed Section 144, banning gatherings, yet protests continue to grow.
  • Raj Thackeray warned against disruptions, while Uddhav criticized the government's arrogance.

Thackerays Declare Joint March as Student Protests Spread

Shiv Sena (UBT) chief Uddhav Thackeray and Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) president Raj Thackeray on Thursday announced a joint morcha in Mumbai on July 26, demanding accountability over the NEET paper leak scandal and condemning the police crackdown on student demonstrators.

https://x.com/yespunjab/status/2080208762032570388

The march will start from Shivaji Park in Dadar and culminate at the Siddhivinayak temple — a symbolically charged route through the heart of Mumbai. The two leaders said no political party flags would be carried, framing the protest as a citizens' movement rather than a partisan exercise.

"We will thrash anyone who tries to disrupt our peaceful protest in Mumbai on July 26."

— Raj Thackeray, MNS President

Uddhav Thackeray said he had spoken with Congress leader Rahul Gandhi about the protest, and that Congress leaders from the Maha Vikas Aghadi (MVA) alliance in Maharashtra would participate. The cousins' decision to march together marks a deepening of their political reconciliation, which began in mid-2025 during the Hindi imposition row.

Uddhav Attacks Centre, Draws British Parallel

At a press conference in Delhi earlier this week, Uddhav launched a blistering attack on the Bharatiya Janata Party-led Union government. He called the ruling dispensation "arrogant" for refusing to engage with students and the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement, which has been protesting at Jantar Mantar for over a month demanding Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation over repeated exam paper leaks.

"People are now saying even the British were better. Those in power today have become arrogant, but it will not take the people long to bring that arrogance down."

— Uddhav Thackeray, Shiv Sena (UBT) chief

Thackeray noted that past governments had engaged with protesters — Indira Gandhi met Sonam Wangchuk's father during a hunger strike in Leh, and the UPA government sent union minister Vilasrao Deshmukh to negotiate with Anna Hazare during the anti-corruption movement. "Had the government spoken to Sonam Wangchuk and Abhijeet Dipke when they first approached it, this issue would have been resolved by now," he said.

He also condemned the police action at Jantar Mantar on July 20, alleging that women and children were manhandled. "I saw young girls and women being treated in a manner that has no place in our culture," he said.

Mumbai Protests Escalate Despite Police Crackdowns

The July 26 morcha comes as Mumbai witnesses escalating street protests in solidarity with the Delhi agitation. On July 22, at least 1,500 people marched near Shivaji Park despite being denied permission to assemble there, according to The Hindu Business Line. The crowd grew so large that police could not estimate its size.

Mumbai Police have imposed prohibitory orders under Section 144 from July 23 to August 6, banning gatherings of five or more persons without permission. According to Madhyamam, police have registered FIRs against more than 50 people in connection with solidarity protests at Chaityabhoomi in Dadar, with cases filed at Mahim and Shivaji Park police stations under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and the Maharashtra Police Act.

Despite the crackdown, Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Aditya Thackeray appeared at the end of the July 22 march and called for another gathering on July 24. Actor Imran Khan, who attended the protest, told The Hindu Business Line: "I feel the people who criticise the students in this way hold the children to a higher accountability than the established authorities."

A Broader Movement Takes Shape

The CJP-led movement at Jantar Mantar, which began as an online satire campaign in May, has grown into what Reuters described as "a rare display of public dissent against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government." The movement demands Pradhan's resignation over repeated test paper leaks, and gained momentum after activist Sonam Wangchuk began an indefinite hunger strike in support.

The Jantar Mantar encampment endured a major police crackdown on July 20 — the opening day of Parliament's Monsoon Session — when tens of thousands of mostly young people tried to march toward Parliament. Police deployed tear gas and batons to disperse the crowd. By July 22, the protest site swelled to 5,000 people despite intermittent monsoon showers, sustained by food deliveries from supporters across India and the diaspora.

The Mumbai University Senate on July 22 accepted a memorandum from Yuva Sena members supporting the NEET protesters and passed a resolution condemning the police action, according to Careers360.

What's Next

Political Dynamics in Mumbai
›Joint march signifies political reconciliation between Thackeray cousins.
›Congress leaders from MVA alliance expected to join.
›Uddhav criticized the ruling government for its handling of protests.

The July 26 morcha will test whether the Thackerays' combined mobilization can sustain pressure on the BJP-led government in both Maharashtra and Delhi. The march is planned despite Section 144 prohibitions, setting up a potential confrontation with Mumbai Police. Opposition parties are also expected to coordinate strategy on the NEET crisis during Parliament's ongoing Monsoon Session, with Uddhav and Rahul Gandhi reportedly discussing joint approaches.

For the Modi government, the expanding protest movement poses a growing challenge as it draws support from students, parents, opposition politicians, and cultural figures — constituencies that cut across traditional political divides.
